Learning Objectives By the end of this session, you will be able to: Explain the concept and value of federated identity Define federated identity and describe how it addresses cross-domain authentication needs. Illustrate its benefits in user experience, security, and governance. Understand Single Sign-On (SSO) and how it works Explain what SSO is, how it reduces login friction, and how it relates to federated identity. Compare SSO-enabling protocols and their use cases Describe the structure and flows of SAML , OAuth2 , and OpenID Connect . Map each protocol to appropriate real-world scenarios. Apply concepts through practical hands-on configuration Use Keycloak to implement OIDC SSO across multiple applications. Federate Keycloak with an external IdP (e.g., Google). Outcome: You will understand the motivations behind federated identity and SSO, master the associated protocols, and gain hands-on experience configuring secure, scalable identity federation systems.

Federated Identity – "Who you are and how your identity is trusted across domains" Federated Identity is a model of identity management where multiple distinct identity systems (e.g., from different organizations or domains) establish mutual trust to allow a user to authenticate in one domain and access resources in another without re-registering or managing separate credentials. Key Characteristics: • Based on trust relationships between Identity Providers (IdPs) and Service Providers (SPs). • The user's identity is managed by one domain but accepted by others. • Often uses standards like SAML, OIDC , or WS-Federation to transfer identity claims. • Identity Federation is the process of setting up and managing this trust. Examples: • Logging into a university library system using your university's central account. • An enterprise using Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) to access partner tools from another vendor.

Single Sign-On (SSO) – "How many times you have to authenticate" Definition: Single Sign-On is an authentication mechanism that allows a user to log in once and gain access to multiple applications or services without needing to log in again during the session. Key Characteristics: • SSO may operate within a single domain or across federated domains . • The goal is to minimize repeated login prompts while maintaining secure sessions. • Achieved through session tokens, cookies, or authentication assertions . • Commonly implemented using protocols like SAML, OIDC, Kerberos , etc.
Single Sign-On is an authentication mechanism that allows a user to log in once and gain access to multiple applications or services without needing to log in again during the session.

• SSO may operate within a single domain or across federated domains . • The goal is to minimize repeated login prompts while maintaining secure sessions. • Achieved through session tokens, cookies, or authentication assertions . • Commonly implemented using protocols like SAML, OIDC, Kerberos , etc.

SAML Flow (SP-Initiated): 1. Bob wants a beer 1. Bob goes first to the Beer Tent (Service Provider) . 2. Beer Tent says: "Go get a wristband!" and redirects Bob to the Wristband Tent with a note (SAML request). 2. Bob goes to the Wristband Tent (Identity Provider) 1. Bob shows his ID (logs in). 2. If approved, he receives a wristband (SAML assertion). 3. Bob is redirected back to the Beer Tent . 3. At the Beer Tent 1. The Beer Tent sees the wristband. 2. It checks: 1. Is it valid? 2. Is it signed by the trusted Wristband Tent? 3. If yes, Bob is served beer (granted access). SP-Initiated Authentication Flow The diagram illustrates the SP-Initiated Authentication Flow involving three main entities: User, Service Provider, and Identity Provider. Flow Steps: ① Request access to resource (Service Provider to User) ② redirected to SAML IdP with SAML Request (Service Provider to Identity Provider) ③ Ask authentication (Identity Provider to User) ④ Provide credentials (User to Identity Provider) ⑤ SAML assertion (Identity Provider to Service Provider) ⑥ Verify assertion (Service Provider to Identity Provider) ⑦ Deliver resource to user (Service Provider to User) Service Provider Verification Questions: Signature → Can I trust it? Issuer → Who created it? Audience → Who is it for? Subject → How/where is it used? Time → Is it still valid? Replay → Is it reused? Decryption → Can I read it securely? SAML Key Components of SAML: Assertions Data packets sent by the IdP to the SP to provide information about the user's identity and permissions. Types include Authentication Assertion, Attribute Assertion, and Authorization Decision Assertion. Identity Provider (IdP) Authenticates users and generates SAML assertions. Example: A corporate identity server or an external provider like Okta. Service Provider (SP) Receives the SAML assertion from the IdP and grants the user access to its services. Example: A web application or software service. SAML Advantages: 🔒 Centralized Authentication Users authenticate once with the IdP, streamlining the login process. ♥ Security Credentials are not shared with the SPs, reducing exposure to potential breaches. 📦 Scalability Supports seamless authentication across multiple SPs in enterprise environments.

OAuth2 Protocol The diagram illustrates the OAuth2 Protocol flow. A central user icon (a person with a thumbs up) is connected to four main components: the Client Application, the Resource Server, the Authorization Server, and the Resource Owner. The Client Application is shown as a laptop with a document icon. The Resource Server is shown as a server rack with a document icon. The Authorization Server is shown as a server rack with a document icon. The Resource Owner is shown as a server rack with a document icon. The flow is as follows: 1. The Client Application requests access from the Resource Owner. 2. The Resource Owner issues an access token to the Client Application. 3. The Client Application uses the access token to request access from the Resource Server. 4. The Resource Server grants access to the Client Application. 5. The Client Application also interacts with the Authorization Server, which verifies the user's identity and issues access tokens to the client application. Diagram of the OAuth2 Protocol flow OAuth2 - Delegated access OAuth2 is a token-based authorization protocol that enables secure access to resources on behalf of a user without exposing their credentials. Key Concepts of OAuth2: • Resource Owner: The user who owns the data or resources being accessed. • Client Application: The third-party application requesting access to the resource owner's data. • Authorization Server: Verifies the user's identity and issues access tokens to the client application. • Resource Server: Hosts the protected data or resources that the client application wants to access. Token types • Access Token: Used by the client application to access protected resources. • Refresh Token: Used to obtain a new access token without requiring user reauthentication. Advantages of OAuth2: Shield icon representing security Secure Authorization: User credentials are never exposed to client applications. Gears icon representing granular permissions Granular Permissions: Users can control the scope of access granted to client applications. Globe icon representing wide adoption Wide Adoption: Supported by many APIs and platforms like Google, Facebook, and GitHub.

How OAuth2 Supports Federation and Delegated Access OAuth2 is a token-based authorization protocol that enables secure access to resources on behalf of a user without exposing their credentials. Bob owns a vault at the bank. (1) Fran is a lawyer Bob wants to act on his behalf. (2) Bob contacts the Authorization Desk (Auth Server) and says: "Allow Fran to access my vault, but only to see documents, not withdraw cash." (3) The desk gives Fran an access slip (access token). (4) Fran goes to the Vault Clerk (Resource Server) and shows the slip. Clerk checks: • Is this slip valid? • Is Fran allowed to view (not edit)? • Is it for Bob's vault? (5) If all pass → access granted ✅. (Actually, Fran gets an authorization code first, then she exchange it for an access token ) The diagram illustrates the OAuth2 flow for delegated access between three main entities: Bob, Fran (Client), and the Bank's services (Authorization Desk and Vault Clerk). Bob (Owner) is represented by a person icon. Fran (Client) (Lawyer) is represented by a person icon. Authorization Desk (Auth Server) is represented by a person at a desk with a "BANK" sign. Vault Clerk (Resource Server) is represented by a vault door icon. The flow is numbered 1 through 5: (1) Fran asks Bob: "Can I access docs?" (2) Bob sends a request to the Authorization Desk: "Allow Fran to access my vault, but only to see documents, not withdraw cash." (3) The Authorization Desk sends an "access slip" (access token) to Fran. (4) Fran sends the access slip to the Vault Clerk. (5) The Vault Clerk grants access to Fran, returning documents to her. Diagram illustrating the OAuth2 flow for delegated access.

Authorization Code Grant The diagram illustrates the Authorization Code Grant flow between four components: Resource Owner (Browser), Client App, Auth Server, and Resource Server. The flow is as follows: 1. The Resource Owner (Browser) clicks "Login". 2. The Client App redirects the Resource Owner (Browser) to the Auth Server. 3. The Resource Owner (Browser) is redirected to the Auth Server login page. 4. The Auth Server returns a login form to the Resource Owner (Browser). 5. The Resource Owner (Browser) enters their credentials and submits them to the Auth Server. 6. The Auth Server authenticates the user and redirects back to the Client App with an authorization code. 7. The Client App requests an access token from the Auth Server using the authorization code. 8. The Auth Server validates the code and returns an access token to the Client App. 9. The Client App makes an API request to the Resource Server using the access token. 10. The Resource Server validates the token and returns an API response to the Client App. 11. The Client App receives the API response from the Resource Server. Key events and data flows: Code: The authorization code is passed from the Auth Server to the Client App (Step 6). Access token: The access token is returned from the Auth Server to the Client App (Step 8) and used by the Client App to request data from the Resource Server (Step 9). Sequence diagram of the Authorization Code Grant flow. Authorization Code Grant (Recommended for Most Apps)

Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) An additional security layer on top of the authorization code grant flow, ensuring that the application that starts the authentication flow is the same one that finishes it Problem of authorization code flow : Code interception The diagram illustrates the Authorization Code Grant flow with PKCE, highlighting a security vulnerability. It features four main components: Resource Owner (Browser), Client App, Auth Server, and Resource Server. Flow Steps: 1. Resource Owner (Browser) Clicks Login. 2. Redirect to Client App. 3. To auth server login. 4. The auth server returns login form. 5. The user enters their credentials and submits them to the auth server. 6. Auth user and redirect with code. 7. To app with code. 8. Code (intercepted by Malicious app). 9. Validates and return access token. 10. Access token. 11. Validate token, API response. Security Vulnerability: A Malicious app is shown intercepting the Code (Step 8) and the Access token (Step 10) before they reach the Client App. This is labeled as "Code interception". Flow Labels: Click Login Redirect To auth server login The user enters their credentials and submits them to the auth server To app with code Code Access token Validate token, API response Client App Actions: Redirect Validates and return access token Auth Server Actions: The auth server returns login form Auth user and redirect with code Validates and return access token Resource Server Action: Validate token, API response Authorization Code Grant (Recommended for Most Apps) Diagram of the Authorization Code Grant flow with PKCE, showing a malicious app intercepting the code.

How OpenID Connect Enables Federated Authentication Bob owns a vault at the bank. (1) Fran is a lawyer Bob wants to act on his behalf. (2) Bob contacts the Authorization Desk (Identity Provider) and says: "Authorize Fran to access my vault records, and issue a signed ID card to prove I approved this." (3) The Bank Access Desk ask Bob's Id (authentication). (4) After verification, the desk gives Fran an access slip (access token) and an Id Token proves Bob's identity and consent. (5) Fran goes to the Vault Clerk (Resource Server) and shows the slip (access token). Clerk checks: • Is this slip valid? • Is Fran allowed to view (not edit)? • Is it for Bob's vault? (6) If all pass → access granted ✓. ①②③④⑤⑥⑦⑧⑨ The diagram illustrates the OpenID Connect federated authentication process involving four main entities: Bob, Fran (Relying Party), the Authorization Desk (Identity Provider), and the Vault Clerk (Resource Server). Bob is represented by a man in a green shirt. Fran (Relying Party) is represented by a woman in an orange shirt. Authorization Desk (Identity Provider) is represented by a man in a blue suit at a desk with a "BANK" sign. Vault Clerk (Resource Server) is represented by a vault door. The process follows these steps: (1) Fran asks Bob, "Can I access docs?" (2) Bob contacts the Authorization Desk, requesting authorization for Fran to access his vault records and a signed ID card. (3) The Authorization Desk asks Bob for authentication (ID verification). (4) After verification, the Authorization Desk issues Fran an access slip (access token) and an Id Token (proving Bob's identity and consent). (5) Fran goes to the Vault Clerk and shows the access slip. (6) The Vault Clerk checks the slip and grants access if all checks pass. Arrows indicate the flow of requests, tokens, and access grants between the entities. How OpenID Connect Enables SSO Bob owns 2 vaults at the bank. • Vault A: Financial records (used by Fran) • Vault B: Insurance policies (used by Alice) All vaults are managed by different Vault Clerks (Resource Servers). They all trust the same Bank Access Desk (Identity Provider). (1) Fran is a lawyer: "Can I access your financial vault? And prove it's really you who approved this?" Bob contacts the Authorization Desk (Identity Provider) and says: "Authorize Fran to access my vault A records, and issue a signed ID card to prove I approved this." The Bank Access Desk asks Bob's Id (authentication). After verification, the desk gives Fran an access slip (access token) and an Id Token proves Bob's identity and consent. (5) Fran goes to the Vault Clerk A (Resource Server A) and shows the slip. (6) Clerk checks the slip: If all pass → access granted ✅. So far, same steps as before (steps 2-4 are not shown anymore for clarity of the diagram) (7) Alice (Bob's insurance agent): "I need to see your insurance vault." (8) Bob is redirected again to the same Bank Access Desk (9) Since he is already authenticated, the Bank Access Desk immediately issues a new authorization code for Vault B. (10) – (11) Alice exchanges it and accesses Vault B — without Bob logging in again This is Single Sign-On — Bob logs in once, and that authentication is reused across multiple trusted services. OIDC Authentication Flows Authentication Flows Description Authorization Code Flow Exchanges an authorization code for tokens via the backend — secure and recommended. Implicit Flow (deprecated) Returns tokens directly in the browser — now deprecated due to security risks. Hybrid Flow Combines frontchannel and backchannel token delivery for flexible response patterns Device Authorization Flow (Device Code Flow) Authenticates users on devices without browsers via a second device Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication (CIBA) Authenticates the user on a separate trusted channel without user interaction on the client.

Real-World Use Cases Federated identity and SSO are widely adopted in various domains, enhancing user experiences and streamlining access across systems. These technologies are integral to modern authentication and access management solutions. 1. Consumer Applications • Example: A user logs into services like Spotify, Airbnb, and Medium with their Google account. • Outcome: Simplifies user onboarding and improves retention by reducing barriers to access. 3. Government Services • Example: A citizen uses their government-issued digital ID to file taxes, renew a passport, and access healthcare services. (France Connect) • Outcome: Improves service delivery and simplifies interactions between citizens and government agencies. 5. E-Commerce and Payment Systems • Example: A shopper uses their PayPal account to log into various online stores and make payments. • Outcome: Improves customer satisfaction and fosters trust in e-commerce platforms. 2. Healthcare Systems • Example: A doctor logs into a hospital portal to view electronic health records (EHR) and access lab results using a single set of credentials. • Outcome: Enhances efficiency and ensures compliance with data protection regulations like HIPAA. 4. Educational Institutions • Example: A student logs into a university portal to access course materials, submit assignments, and register for classes. • Outcome: Enhances the educational experience and streamlines resource management for administrators.

Key Concepts: • Federated Identity: • System for sharing identity information between trusted domains • Enables seamless access across systems • Single Sign-On (SSO): • One-time authentication for multiple application access • Improves convenience and security 2.
